blocks.x: This is Joe Phillips. That's loud enough.
Yes, that's good. When were you born? How old are you?
Well, I'm 65. You can just sit back. Tell them your age. You can just sit back. Just take it easy. Lean back.
Tell them your right age. Now you know you ain't 65. What year were you born in?
That's one thing. I don't know much.

He's 78 years old right now. 78 years? 78 years old. Well, you've got a good age already now. And were you born here in the city? No, I was born in St. John's Parish. In St. John's Parish. And when did you leave St. John's Parish?
1918. You left St. John's Parish. See? Now, what was the first kind of music you heard that you remember? Any type of music?
When I first come to the city?
No, when you first started out when you were a little boy. In the country.
In the country. Well, when I was in the country, I was playing guitar. In a band.
Oh, yeah.
A band by the name of the Magnolia Band. I was playing guitar. The Magnolia. The Magnolia Band.
And, who was the leader of the band?
Well, it was a first cousin of mine. It was a young man by the name of Casimir Matthews. I was the leader.
Casimir Matthews.
He was the leader of the band. The Magnolia Band.
Did he have a manager, too?
Huh? Was he the manager, too? He was the manager. He was the manager? He was the violin player. He was the manager. I see.
And what towns did you play in?
Oh, I played with the Lord in so many towns. Or in the country.
Uh-huh.
I played St. James. I played St. John. I played St. Charles Parish.
Uh-huh.
Play music all different places. We are at Dansonville. When I was out there.
Up in Playman Williams territory.
That's right. Playman Williams, please. Out there.

I talked to Freddie Landry up there about a year ago, the trombone play. You remember him? I remember him. Play trombone and piano? I remember him. I think his brother's name was Al C. You remember the big boy? Yeah. He came down here and worked with the Eureka Band. Remember all those fellas from up there?
That's right.
Who else was in this Magnolia Band? How big a band was it?
Seven-piece band.
It was a seven-piece band?
Seven-piece band. And who else was in it?
And who else was in it? If I wait. Instrumentation did they have? You know, different instruments?
Well, they had a fella they called Fernand Alexander. That was the trumpet player. And the other boy, the trombone player, and the name's No-No Lagrange. No-No Lagrange.
That's right.

The drummer was Romeo L. Thomas. And the other boy, and I don't forget the boy play guitar. I don't forget his name. But anyway, the first name was Noon. But the last name I forgot was about the guitar player.
And what instrument were you playing?
Bass violin. In that band? In that band.
Did they have a saxophone or a clarinet? Yeah?
They had a clarinet.
They had a clarinet.
Clarinet.

And about how old were you when this was? Do you remember what year it was? Anything approximately when you started out? Long time, long time ago. Long time ago. Was it before the Spanish-American War?
Oh, yeah. Long time ago.
Well, did they read music in those days?
No, no, no, no. They said, some of them just sold me. Valid. Valid. Not like they do now. Fair enough. Valid.
Well, did they play? Did they have to play by ear? Or how did they make it?
That's right. That's right. They tough it all by ear like that.
No, I ain't know nothing about it. You know I got to fix myself. I kind of got slaggy.
Well, the first time I see the music they were reading, everything, you understand? That went out when I stuck them all in.
Oh, I see. Those bands didn't read out of the country.
Yeah, you know, sometimes they had about one or two could read a little bit something. The rest of them, they just took play just by ear like that the best way they could. They could.
Well, even, how old were you when you started playing music?
Oh, Lord, don't tell you the truth. When I started to play music, I was very young.
Very young.
Very young, all of us.
You mean about 10 or 12, something like that, or younger than that?
No, older than that.
Old than that, about 16 or something?
Something like that. We all was young when we started, when we put up the Magnolia Band.
Well, that'd be about, let's see. When were you, what year were you born again? About 1889. About 1889.
That'd be about 1905. No, wait a minute. I think I'm making a mistake here. About 1870 now.
Yeah. About 1870. That'd be about 1895. Would you mind if I turned the radio down? Oh, I can. I'll turn it off. I got a pop phone. I'll turn it off. I can hear it in here. Yeah.
Well, let me turn around. I think you can see me a little better now. Yeah. You can understand what I say better.
So, before you started playing yourself, do you remember hearing music around in the country?
Yes, they had music around the country.
What kind of music did you hear?
Well, they had a history from Laplace. Uh-huh. On this side of the river. They used to come and play dance out there. You used to hear them, you know. And they had a brass band, too.
They did?
On this side of Laplace. But why was they crossed the river?
Oh, yes. What did they play? What kind of tunes? Do you remember any of the tunes?
Oh, Lord. They used to play all the best way they could. But just by a year like that, they didn't read music. No. I'll tell you the truth about that.
Did they have any just guys wandering around playing guitar alone in those days?
No. No. I used to see something like that around the place when they come on this side of the river, but not where I was. The fellow played guitar, he played in the band.
Oh, I see. They played in the band.
In the band.
Did they play any jazz that far back? Or was it mostly waltzes and things like that?
That's it. The card drill and everything. They used to play all that.
Did they play any ragtime?
That's right. They used to play the best way they came. Well, they were called a pretty good little band because that's all they had out there.
Did they play any numbers like blues numbers?
Yeah.
In those days?
Yeah, they used to play the blues and things, but not like they don't like the down in town when I come in the city. Because when I first come in the city, I got in a blues band, sure enough.
Oh, yeah. Yeah. So they played blues even in the country before you came into the city.
That's right.
Mm-hmm.
Now, who are some of the other country bands you played with before you came to the city?
Well, I didn't. I played a few jobs with the band from Laplace sometime. When the bass player took sick, they come and got me. I played a few jobs with them.
Mm-hmm. And what was the name of that band?
That band, that band there, or the Pickwick. Oh, the Pickwick? The Pickwick. Then I played with them. A few jobs when the bass player took sick.
And?
Then after that, I came in the all in. Mm-hmm.
Who was in that band, the Pickwick band?
Well, they had a, they was mixed up. Settle and Youngster, they was mixed up. They had a seven-piece orchestra too. But they had a brass band.
That was a brass band? The Pickwick band?
Uh-huh. The brass band and orchestra. They had both. They had both.
Did you know Kip Thomas, I've been? Well, his family.
Oh, I didn't know the family so good, but I've been know Kip Thomas.
Oh.
I had that before he left there.
Mm-hmm. Did they have many good musicians, like the Hall? Did you know the Hall boys?

Oh, sure, sure. I know one of them by the name of Edward Hall. There was a clarinet player. He was playing the Pickwick brass band. One of the best clarinet players they had out there. On the place. Mm-hmm. And I'd know Thomas for a long time before Thomas come to town.
Oh, yeah. Well, this Edward Hall, was that the father?
That was the father. That was the father. Lot of, lot of, yeah, he had a lot of children.
And do you remember the names of the children? Do you remember them very well?
Well, there's one come here in the city, was playing, I was playing saxophone. And I couldn't remember his name. I know he was playing alto saxophone, the one he sung.
That's Robert and Clarence and Edmund.
Edmund, I believe that's the one who was playing saxophone.
Edmund, he's with Louis Armstrong.
Yeah.
He joined a little song.
And then he had another tall one, I don't forget his name, was a good musician too.
That's, that's Edmund, he's the tall one.
Must be.
He used to work with Buddy Petit around here.
That's right.
He went to Florida.
That's right.
What, before you, did you start out with a regular guitar when you were about 16 or did you make your own instrument before then?

I started with the guitar, you see. But there's lots of children. The fellow's leader was cutting them in mine, you see. My mother's sister's boy. He was the leader. And he put me on the guitar. And the party, they put the boy, I'll tell you about the name Newman on bass. And he couldn't make it. I see. So my cousin begged me to, to, to, to swap with him. So I took the bass and he took guitar.
Did he teach you? Your cousin?
No, well, he, he, you know, he was playing violin. I see. He was playing violin. But I got, I got right away, first class on that bass.
So you learned it pretty much by yourself.
Oh, that's right. That's right. Just, just head like that. Mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm.

I was, I, I told them, I said, my cousin begged me to take the, the bass. I tell them, I'll take that bass. You know, you need no automobile, one thing, another one, to go play different place. I say, if you all, when we got to go play, if you all help me to tote that thing, I'll take it.
How should, how did you go around with it? Did you have a wagon or?
Well, sometimes we had one new car.
Uh-huh.
Like that, a buggy.
Uh-huh.
And house. No automobile. No.
What kind of things, what kind of, did you play dances and parties and things like that?
Yeah, we used to, we used to play out there for white and color. Different place, different people, you know, white and color.
Did you ever have any brass band work? Ever do any brass band work? No.
No, never.
You always played dance, huh?

Yeah, we danced all the time, all the time. When the society, you used to have some kind of tutel, something like that, to get the band on this side, it looked like the brass band. We didn't have no brass band.
I see. What kind of dances did you play for?

All them society, you know, St. Mitchell's Society, St. Paul, a lot of people like that. Different, different society. Mm-hmm. We played dance for them. And then we played a dance for white people many times.
What kind of dances would they have?
Same kind? They used to have a dance in a hall like that. Picnics. They played the same music? Fabo? Everything. Fabo. Fabo, everything. I see.
I see. Were there any special places that they had for picnics out there? Any kind of parks or anything?

Well, there's one place, the people used to, it was a bond family. They used to have a hall, and then sometimes a whole lot of trees. They used to give under the pecan tree, one thing and another, under the tree, give big picnics in the summertime.
Where was the band then? Where did the band play? Under the tree?
Under the tree, too.
You didn't have a bandstand?
No, no bandstand. No bandstand under the tree.
People danced there?
And they used to jump, you know, everything out there.
On the grass, or did they have some kind of thing to dance on?
Just on the outside, they're on the grass.
They have tables around?
All around.
No.
All around, table, plenty, plenty of table, a lot of things to eat and drink.
Everybody bring their own food, or could you come and buy?
They bring baskets, you see?
Mm-hmm.
Everybody.
And some beer or something like that?
That's right, Dad. Well, they had a lot of liquor and everything.
Everybody brought their own, though.
That's right. They had plenty fun out there.
Well, what happened after the picnic goes on for a while? Did the band change its style any? Did they get more ratty, or?
Well, sometimes they give us a rest, you see? A rest to eat. Oh, I see. And then they got to go back. They give you a rest to eat, you know.
I see. And you played some ragtime?

No. No. Oh, yeah. The New World days, everybody that was crazy about our little band, they couldn't do no better. They didn't like no more. Oh, yeah. You see? And the New Orleans band would have cost them too much.
Yeah. Well, did you hear many New Orleans bands in the country?
Well, when they had a big to do, what they call a banque for the society.
Oh, yeah.
They get a band and this is like a rainy. Okay. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.

Kid Howard, Jack Carey, all bands like that. They get a different band just for that day. They call that a bonké. They start on Saturday. Free eating and dance and everything out there for the society. That's the only time they get a New Orleans band.
Did those fellows help you any or did you mostly learn from country fellows?
They just heard that from country fellow.
Mm-hmm.
Yes, of course, I learned a whole lot is when I come to the city.
Yes, well, when you were young, did you watch any of the old bass players?
Oh, yeah, they had one from Laplace. What was his name? His name was Joe Robinet. Joe Robinet. He got drunk.
Did he play by ear?
Well, he used to read.
Oh, he was a reader.
Yeah, he used to read. He used to play that with Laplace Orchestra.
Did he use a bow or did he play flat?
Well, he used to. He used to use bow. All of us used to use bow, you understand?
Mm-hmm.
Now, that picking bass like that, I just started this thing when I got to New Orleans. Oh, I see. Because everybody else was doing it.
They didn't do that in the country?
No, not in the country. They used a bow. Mm-hmm. And people was crazy about a bow.
Well, it sounds nice today when they don't want to waltz.
That's right. But they got some bass players in New Orleans right now that they don't know how to use a bow. They never use a bow. That's true. But I used bow. But I used bow.
It sounded good over in Hope's Hall. Remember?
That's right.
When we were over there with Kit Thomas. It sounded nice on the record. That bow came through. You ought to hear it. I might hear it. Any other older men help you when you were young?
Well, just like I tell you, just two fellas from this side of you, they were from Laplace.
And what was the other one's name?
The trumpet player by the name of Dajon. Dajon. His name was Dajon. He was the trumpet player. But he used to give me a hard job on playing music, you know?
Is he related to Harold Dajon, the clarinet and saxophone player? You know the saxophone player Harold Dajon from his?
Oh, yeah, I know this one. But there was no can. No can. No can. But there were two brothers, Dajon and Joe. Both of them would play trumpet at Laplace. And they would help you play on your bass?
Yeah, on the band, you know.

But only the man I had to all the time talk to me about my bass, give me a hard job with the bass player in that band at Laplace. The fellas was going to play a dance at my home in St. Paul Hall. And they were in the skiff. And a big wind come. It's like a storm like that in the middle of the river.
In the middle of the river.

Everybody got, let me see, there were seven in a great big skiff. They were going there to play that dance. Everybody got done except one. Really? Except one. They were going, everybody was waiting for them, for that beat to do there. That skiff in the middle of the river turn over.
Must have been a terrible storm.
That was terrible weather caught them on that river. Everybody except one. They had all the instruments with them and everything.
Everything. Everything.
Everything. Everything. And in fact, there was a time out there in the country when nothing happened.
What was it, a thunderstorm or something like that?

It was something like that. Or a windstorm or what? It was a thunder and wind. That was a terrible day when that thing happened. And a boy from the coastal river, from Mahon, went to get them in that skiff. One of them great big skiff. New skiff. That skiff just turned over. A boy by the name John, young man.
He went out to get them?
He went out to get them.
In another skiff?
In that same skiff, you see. Where they all got in that skiff and put the instruments and everything. They was well load all right now.
Yeah.
And the skiff turned over. Of course, he got drawn too.
Well, he went over in the skiff to pick them up. That's right.
I see. And he got drawn too.
Gee.
He got drawn too. It was a bad day.
Yeah.
One, if I'm not mistaken, I did the trombone play. I got saved.
Did he swim back or did he just hang on to the boat?
He hang on. The boat was turned over. He got to that boat until somebody else come there. He just saved him. That's the only one.
What was the name of that band?
That, let me see. I really used to name that by that trumpet play, by Dajon. Oh, I see. The Kid Dajon band. And they were all right too. It was a sad time over there.
Did you know Kid Ory out there?
Oh, Lord. I used to know the whole family. Kid Ory was a trombone player. And he was a trombone player too when he was down in the city.
Did you hear him in the country?
Oh, yeah.
You knew him and worked with him out there?
Ory?
Yeah. Did you work playing the same band?
No, no. No, no. Ory was on this side. He'd already come in. I was on the other side. He was on this side of the room.
Oh, I see. La Place is on the other side.
You see? La Place. La Place and St. John, you see?
What's the county seat of St. John's? Eh? What's the county seat of St. John's Parish?
St. John's Parish? Yes.
What does the parish seat, you know? The main town there.
Edgar, the town of Edgar. Edgar, you know.
St. John is the parish seat.
Yes, St. John's Parish, you see? Yes. And the post office. Lucy's post office in St. John. And you're from the town of Edgar.
That's right.
That's right. Lucy is right across from La Place. Oh, I see.
It's right across from La Place. Right across from La Place. It's near reserve and it's in that neighborhood, but across the river.
That's right. I see. You see? I did like to see how my wife saved me. Most of the people call that place over there, when you're going to the country like that, Edgar, Louisiana, you know?
Mm-hmm. And you were born right there in that town.
That's right.
I see. Well, were there any other bands, you know, up along the river? Like, what are some of those other towns along in there near Edgar? Well... Honville? Did they have any bands in Honville?

Honville, that's St. John Parish. They did not remember no band there. Mm-hmm. And, uh... Well, the young fellow had a young little band in St. James Parish. You know? Of course, there wasn't much. St. James next to St. John. Mm-hmm. Gone up. Gone up.
I see. And what town did they play around in there, in St. James?
Well, they used to play little dance like that, you know. Mm-hmm. They would not sit down. Because many times when they get... That's Vashery is right there?
Yeah, that's right.
Vashery right there, St. James. I see. St. James Parish. That's it. Mm-hmm.
And what was the name of that band?

That band, I never remember the name of it. They band, but it's a set of young kids. And many times they used to give a dance, they'd get us. Mm-hmm. When the society had a big dance, they'd get us from St. John. So...
What made you decide to come into town?

In the city? Mm-hmm. Well, I tell you, I got disgusted out there. And just make up my mind. Well, most of all my people... Yeah, family problems. And then I had... Well, I just had the family trouble too. But most of all my people was in town. Sister, mother, and everybody. Brother. So I just make up my mind to come. And then I had a bad family trouble too, just like she said.
You know George Foster out there in the country? He's from up around Macau, further up the river.
No, but I heard something about her name like that. George Foster.
He came into the city later, and then he went on up to Chicago and New York. I think he's out in San Francisco now. Oh, yeah. He's out there working with a little man.
I also heard about that name.

Oh, yeah. I met him down here. He came down. His mother was sick. He came down to... See, and he was playing with a Papa Salas fans band. Oh, yeah. They call him Pops Foster too. Foster. Willie Foster's his brother used to get to all that.
Oh, Willie.
Well, they used to work on the boat. That's right. Did you ever hear any of the fans on the boats when they came by?
Oh, I sure did. I sure did. I was the man you talk about a while ago. I played with him. Willie Foster, Celestine. Mm-hmm.
And did you work with him on the boat? No, no.
I worked a few dance with Celestine in the city. Oh, I see. When Louis left here, I played the last dance with him.
Oh, yes. Louis Armstrong.
Louis Armstrong was playing second trumpet with Celestine. Mm-hmm. I played the last dance with them on Carlton Avenue in Maple. And the week after that, they tell me Louis is gone.
Oh, I hear you.
Celestine was playing first trumpet and Louis was playing the second trumpet in the Tuxedo band.
Mm-hmm. And who was in the band then?
That's right.
You remember who the trombone player was?
Bebe Risley.
Oh, I haven't seen him since Celestine's here.
He's living uptown still, didn't he? Somebody tell me he's a deacon in church. He's a deacon?
In church.
That's what they tell me.
He must have put music down.
Yeah, because most sure my wife know him because... How do you play in the church?
Oh, he plays trombone in the church? In the church, yeah. Mm-hmm. Well, that would be nice to hear. I bet he sounds good. Mm-hmm.

And the cause that night, the cause for me to go with them, I wouldn't live so far from that schoolhouse. And the bass player named Jimmy Johnson. Oh, yeah. He took six. They tell me I drink a whole lot of whiskey and eat cabbage, something like that. He took six. And the place was jam and pack up that schoolhouse. Oh, yeah. And he took six, they brought him to the hospital. And Bebe come at my house to get me. Mm-hmm. To finish that dance. And that's the last time I played with Louis Armstrong. And he left. And I was in the week after Louis was gone up north.
What did he sound like then, Louis? What kind of a trumpet player was he? Did he play the same as now or different?

Oh, he was fine. He was first class. He was the first class. Louis was always good. Mm-hmm. But there's a lot of people say he shouldn't play the second trumpet in the tuxedo. He should play the first trumpet. But he told me, he explained to me about it. He told me he couldn't do that because that was Celestine's band. He said, all he wanted is money. Mm-hmm. When he played that was Celestine's band. He said, I can't go be a boss on that man. I just want my money. And they was making money too because they had a first class band and they was playing. They was playing most of the night.
Did Louis play soft or bad?
Louis used to play pretty soft, you know, behind Celestine. Oh, I see.
Yeah. Did they get along well, Louis and Celestine?
Well, they used to get along fine. Fine, that old band. They had a first class band too. Mm-hmm.
Must have been good then.
Oh, they used to play in all them big places. Oh, everywhere in them big places. Night club and I believe country club somewhere. They used to play all them big places.
Was Celestine's band a ragtime band then or was it a reading band? Oh, they had some good reading band there.
In that band I believe most all of them. Mm-hmm.
Most all of them. And did they ever play much by ear? Sometimes.
Sometimes they did. Sometimes they danced. Because they used to play, Celestine used to play for white and color.
Mm-hmm.
Oh, he had a good name and he had a good band too.
Well, how would they work that two trumpet part? Would one of them use a mute and the other one not? Or would they play strict harmony or how would they work it?
You know the first trumpet that was Celestine. Mm-hmm. Celestine used to use the mute multiple times, you see? And Lewis was coming right behind him.
Would Lewis use a mute?
Different, different. Sometime.
Mm-hmm.
Sometime.
Well.
But Lewis was so strong. Mm-hmm.
And Celestine would play the melody then?
That's right. That's right.
And how would Lewis play? Would he play in between the phrases or right underneath Celestine?
In between, you know? That's the way he used to care of that.
Oh. You see? Not just harmony but figures and so on.
That's right. That's how come people used to tell him all the time, he should be blowing the first trumpet. Mm-hmm. And Lewis was a lot young in Celestine too. Oh, yeah.
Yeah. How old was Lewis then do you think about?

Well, Lewis, I tell you too, you see? My wife knows Lewis a whole lot better than me. Right. That's right. Because Lewis used to go to my wife's house and the neighborhood when Lewis was in town. She, she know Lewis. Well, I come to know Lewis by, by being in the Tuxedo band. Oh, I see.
Mm-hmm. But where was your wife brought up? Uh-huh.
Where was your wife born?
Was she born here in the city or in New York? Back to Mississippi. You were born in Mississippi? Back to Mississippi.
Not just Mississippi.

Did you know Walter Vaughn's up there? Yes, I did. He had a good band. I had some records by him. Yeah, my people got big business in Mississippi. I heard that band. The same thing happened to them. They all burned up in a fire except for one band. That's it. That's it. That way, in the rhythm. Who was there? Walter Vaughn's band. Yes. Just like that same deal. They were trying and they all got burned up.
They just had come from play and dance here. Mm-hmm. They was on the way. They went there to play the dance.
You see? That night, it was a baby dog dance. You see?
What?
And where was that? National stuff
And what happened to them?

Well, they said, fellow, you know they had moss in the hall, all dry. You know how they're decorating them Chinese lanterns. And they said some smart aleck throws a cigarette up in the moss, and they'd cock. But a lot of them got out because I have a cousin. He's sharing that. Clutchy got out and got Hattie out. She run back to get a whole straw she had. She just bought a can and wanted to show it out there. She got burned up. Did they have many doors or windows or something? One door.
They nailed up all the windows. They say one door, but they said a lot of people could get saved there if it went through that smoke.
The top of it was tin, you see. And on one side was tin, and the other side was wood. So that tin, they wasn't saying burnt, but they were scalded.
Yeah, the tin got hot.

Yeah, they were scalded. Like in the oven. See, they was pumping that water and that just smothered. I seen a priest, and I love him. He went in that fire and got a girl out there, but she died. But he'd ministered a last sacrament to her. That was Father Booth's natchez. What's a baby doll dance anyhow? You know, the little short dressers. Oh. Was it like a club? Yeah, it was a club. They'd give a baby doll dance, and all the ladies had them short dresses out wide. You know, they called them baby dolls. Just like carnival here.
Mm-hmm. I knew they had them in the city, but I never heard of them out in the natchez. Yeah, yeah.
Mm-hmm.
Well, then the band must have been all the way at the back of the hall. They was. That's why they took a guy out.

They took a guy out because when they first hollered fire, he jumped up and said, play, play, you see? By the time we got round from Pine Street, that place was in a light blaze. My cousin, she was just pulling her hands. She thought her boy was up in that burning place. He had got up.
You mean they played to keep everybody quiet?
Yeah, they thought it was just, you know.
Some poor woman would come out, walk, come out, you see, and forgot a coat in there. A scarf. And something like that went back for it.
And then she never did get out. Mm-mm.
Never did get out. Yeah, don't like it.

All the windows was nailed and bars nailed across them. I was going to say, when they used to give dances, the young boy used to pull them windows to get in free. Yeah. So, uh, this fella, he had an undertaker there, Bob Mack, he went back in there for the money he got burned up. Mm-mm. And left a box, cigar box of money, he got burned up.

What, everybody jammed up against the door and they couldn't get out? Yeah, they just jammed up trying to get out. Charlie Locke told me the only one that got out was the bass player and he walked out carrying his bass with it. Walked out and just kept his head and pushed his way with it. Push his way with it. Hey, Phillip. It's March 25, 1957, reel 2. Play those red hook numbers. Mm-mm.
Yeah, play many dance with love. No. And I played a long time at the night club across the river. That's fake. Oh, yeah. With Thomas. Did you know love in the country? No.
I know Love when I come in the city by playing dance with him.
Mm-mm. And Thomas too. And Thomas too. I love Cross River, I speak. Oh yeah. With Thomas.
Did you know love in the country?
No, I know love when I come in the city by playing dance with him.
Oh, he's from Blackman, you know.
That's right. I used to like love. He was knife, easy trumpet player. And Thomas too.
He told me he used to go up to Baton Rouge. When he was a young man, he used to ride up on his bicycle and play with Toots Johnson's band. Did you ever hear them?
No, I never heard them. I heard them people talk about them. I see.
No, they had several bands in Baton Rouge. Some fella named Victor Tone up there. I thought maybe you'd heard of them. That's right.
The trumpet player. You know what the call to have, I guess. You know Howard Gooden.
Kid Howard? The trumpet player?
The trumpet player.
Oh yeah, I know him well.
Pretty good. I don't know if you ever remember the ball would die. Kid Rene.
I just met him one night.
I played, oh I played a long time with the band. Kid Rene. You know?

It sounded great the night I heard him. He just played one or two tunes right. He's been drinking bad wine and everything, you know. Uh-uh. But he played Royal Garden Blues and Sister Kate and they really sounded good. That's right. He had his lip and everything. Oh Lord. They tell me he could get up above the staff and listen. Yeah, sure right too.
Rene was a nice trumpet player. Uh-huh. Boy looked like old Mexican and he was a nice trumpet player. Rene. Now they mugging and I played with all of them. Sam, Isaiah, Andrew, all of them.
When did you work with Sam?

Oh, that's long time before he died. Uh-huh. Sam had a good band. The people were crazy about Sam. Over the lake. In Mississippi, St. Samuel could stay out there. That band, they were crazy about that band.
Did, uh, was that before he had his brothers in the band or afterwards?
Yeah, he had his brothers in the band. He had his brothers in the band. Uh-huh. Of course they tell me he got the youngest brother playing bass with Cass Calloway, Albert.
Yeah, well he's still playing bass now. I think he's up in Boston, I believe. Last time he was with Sammy Lewis.
The last time I heard they tell me he was playing with Cass Calloway.
Oh, yeah.
What he left then? Albert Morgan. Andrew Morgan, Isaiah and Sam. Four brothers. Yeah. Albert was the youngest one.
Isaiah was sick recently but I hear he's all right now.
Uh, they tell me he got a band across the lake. In Biloxi.
Ah, in Biloxi. I heard, I heard some taints of him but I never heard it in person.
Isaiah.
He's still going strong. He had a fella named Abby Burney's hat that sewed up over there. They got two bands. Oh, yeah.
And Isaiah, Andrew. Oh, they took a minute to dance with him. I see him for a long time. That's how he lost his voice.
He, uh, did you ever travel out in the country much? Huh? Did you ever travel after you came to the city? Did you go to Mississippi? When we were in the country?
Uh-uh. No, no.
Have you ever been to Mississippi and places like that?
Oh, I tell you the truth. I can tell you a place I've been in Mississippi. Did you play in Harris Boyd?
I play in Harris Boyd, Mississippi.

That's Mississippi. Look, I play Harris Boyd, Mississippi. I play in, we play, no we just, we didn't play in Slidell. I went to Slidell, we didn't play in Slidell. We played in Biloxi, Pasch Christian, Pasch Boer, all them place. Whose band was that? All them place there. We play. I used to play with a boy out there going over in Mississippi. Mostly there was two brothers. One named Dude, they had a trumpet player, the other one named Foster. Trombone player, both of them died.
Oh, I knew him, he used to work with Joe Avery.
That's it.
Yeah, he used to work with Till. Avery and Tillman up at the Towers Beer Garden.
That's it. You see that? You know all them, all them, all them, all the truth.
I was down in the Navy about twelve years ago, and I used to go up there and hear him, and he sounded good, you know. I even have a record, he made a homemade record.

I went to, let me see, I believe I just called you, Addisburg, Addisburg, Addisburg in the city, Pasch Boer, at Morgan City. Now I went on a trip with the band, the trumpet player. Got the job with them people, with them white people or whatever. Edgar Sosie, the trumpet player. He got the job. We went to Wichita. You know that, I think.
To Wichita?
Wichita for fall out of the W, that's the name over there. We went there with the Pelican baseball team.
Oh, I see.
We stayed over there two days. Pelican played two games over there with them, and they lost both of them.
Oh, well that sounds like it.
And the week after that, them boys, them same boys, that team, come here.
Oh, yes.

At the Armand Park over there. They played two more games. Pelican lost both. Four games. You played out at the ball game? Over there. Up there with them. In the park, huh? In the park. In the park. Every hearing, we didn't play hard, but we made good money out there.
Did you play in between innings or what?
In between innings like that. In the park?
In the park. In the park. Oh, they used to do that all the time. I'm gonna tell you the truth.

I never see a ball team like that. They had a set of white boys there. Looked to me like most all of them was about six foot and a half, seven foot and a half. Every time they get on bat, it was a home run. Yeah. Never see a ball player like that. Fine set, nine fine young men. Looked like all of them but about the same age.
That must have got everybody pretty upset. I'm telling you the truth.
They make a fool of the pelicans.
Well, we're used to the pelicans lose the hair.

But I'll tell you one thing though. I believe you all were too young to remember that. I'll tell you who the pelicans used to call a first class pitcher. That Italian fella. Joe. Joe something. I wouldn't remember. Joe Martino. Something like that. That pitcher they used to talk so much about. Fazio. Fazio. Fazio. Will I tell you? Them fellas make a fool of him when he got that pitcher stand.
Every time he raised his hand and pitcher go all that part, that ball was out the park. Did you ever play any other baseballs?
No. I don't remember. That pitcher. That pitcher. That pitcher.
That pitcher.
That pitcher. That pitcher. That pitcher. That pitcher.
Did you ever play any other baseball games? No. Who? Were you playing music at many baseball games in those days?
Oh, yeah. Yes, we played music in many, many, many ball places, you know. Yeah, where I was playing ball. Yeah, we played music across the lake where I was at ball games. Yeah.
I had music everywhere in those days. That's right.

They used to play to dance after the baseball open up. It ain't McDonaldville used to call it. Oh, yeah. Well, they had a college baseball park there. They played ball right after the ball game. They'd have a big band. Big dance. Would they go to the hall or would they have a big band? Big dance. Would they go to the hall or would they have a big band? Right out there. In the park?
Mm-hmm. Who'd come? The people, this is for everybody that's playing? The people, people crowded there. Yeah, they'd be crowded out there already.
Mm-hmm.

That's something unusual. I guess you could get the first pace easy that way. You could strike out pretty easy too. I guess you could stay long enough. Yeah. Who played with you over in McDonaldville? Who about? In the ballpark in McDonaldville. Did you work over there? Was he in the band or was he in the band or was he in the band or was he in the band or was he in the band? Yeah, I was standing there. I was standing there. I was standing there.

Oh, I see the bandwagon used to play that. And they used to play penny quarters for Chicken, what's that white man name out there? What? You know, you forget, Lord. The white man, Joe Powell. Oh. They called him Chicken Powell. That's right. Y'all played on Saturday nights for him out there. That's right. In New York.
Sure is.

They used to call him Mr. Chicken Powell. He'd give dances for the color out there in New York. That's right. On Saturday nights. Well, that would be after they'd go to the pay table, long-term, and pay off, you know. Had plenty of money to flash around, and of course the women would be there. And they and them was playing there then. But I wasn't his wife in them days, but I know him. I used to follow up in dances and bands. I had a cousin, Henry Zeno, who used to play. The drummer? With Kid Oliver. That was kin to me. He used to play in the Eager Band, Long Years.

When he was done, he played with Tuxedo. I know. That's when he died. He played with Tuxedo. But I, about 32 cents I've been in New York. I ain't never here about a drummer. That's interesting. Yes, that's interesting. Oh, everybody used to talk somewhat about that boy. Father did, too. That's why he's here.
Yeah.
Yeah. That's when I was first cousin. Mm-hmm. And the other old boy used to play.
That's why I used to follow them dances.
Beautiful. Yeah. Beautiful.
See, they had King Oliver. What did you call him? King Oliver?
King Oliver had that big eye. He used to work at Second Magazine as a butler and used to play music. Well, in them days, that was the Eager Band.
He used to work where as a butler?

Second Magazine. Second Magazine. Well, that was a fancy neighborhood in them days. The Bontong people lived all out there in them days. Then, you see, the Irish town was divided from them. But after...

Excuse me. His first name was Joe Oliver. Joe, I said. But everybody in town didn't have a call. They called him Kid Oliver. Kid Oliver. I don't know. Kid Oliver. Oh, but that man could blow some trumpet.
He had a big eye. That's right. That's right. That's right.
Hmm. Well, was the eye just bigger than the other one or didn't his lid close or something?
No, it didn't close. It was cartridge. It was something that had happened. He didn't see out of that eye.

He didn't? Uh-uh. Well, he didn't have to see to play good anyway. He really could play a little... He could close his eyes and play good. I'm telling you. He didn't have to worry about anything. He didn't have to read. Uh-uh. He didn't have to read. Who was with the... Do you remember the other followers with Kid Oliver? Yeah.

I'll tell you one with William Moshul. You know all of them. I know you know this one. Zeb, the client of mine. Oh, Zeb Lano. Zeb, the one that left you and died. Die up north somewhere. Yeah. Because he left you sick. And when they come to find out, you will get out there.
Listen, I was a lone Frenchman. You too.
and he would run me out the hall. He used to play in that too. But I can't see. He had curly hair and nice looking. Oh.

What a little. You know, he didn't try to call him. That's Frank and Doocy. Yeah. That's what's up. That's a tramp all black. Yeah. Frank and Doocy. That was a slight tramp on you talking about. When you say good hair. That's all they used to call him.
Mm-hmm.
He had hair like silk.
They called him good hair.
Yes, but he was some trombone play. That's all you could hear. Frank and Doocy.
What kind of numbers did he play?
Oh, well, all kind of different music.

Jazz and shotties and waltz and quadrille. That was their main. You see, at 1130 they start the quadrille. You get your partner and I get mine. I guess you've seen that. Swing around the floor. They call that the quadrille. They used to play the shotties for a prize. The one that dance the levelest and the best got a prize. What kind of prizes would he get? Well, sometimes we laid his parasols and watched.

Now, that's what the people used to be crazy about. The people used to cry out there. But Joe Oliver. He eat us on a condom blue. Oh. Oh, yes. This man, Buddy Petit and Punch. Oh, I'm treated at a good... I have a love now somewhere.

No, Punch is here. He's staying at the Page Hotel. Oh, no. That's right. Oh. Punch is here? Yeah. I almost got arrested with another night. I had a headache so I didn't play. Oh. The judge didn't like it. We were mixing it up, you know. Yeah, I know they don't like it.

I almost got arrested with another night. They just don't like it. And it ain't no use of trying to put it over. They don't like it. And it's been going on before you, you, me or him was born. That mix. And they ain't gonna never break it up. Oh, no. Well, I mean, you just gotta sit in. They ain't gonna be friends. They ain't gonna never break that mess up, no, huh? I have a cousin, she might pass here. She's white as you, and no more as my cousin. She's kind of me. Yeah. That's right. And that daddy died. Up there in Natchez. He left property for his wife, Cheryl Lucille. And he left property for her. They couldn't do nothing with him when he's dead. Sure.

I thought the French was standing, it wasn't, I thought it was called the Lachs. It's a Page. I think it's a Page Hotel on that part. Not too far from here. No. But Eddie Morris is playing with him now. You remember Eddie Morris? The trombone player. Morris? Yeah. The trombone player was with him when he had Joe. Georgey Boyd and Johnny and all those fellows. Yeah. He comes back. What you got?
Where you come back now?
He's coming back, he's got a beautiful tull. Lord, Lord. You can phone punch up there.
Phone on the hotel, you still have a show with the right people. The Page Hotel. On Rampo? On Rampo.
Oh, and uh, you know his real name? No. Nobody ever knows his real name. I know.
They got a page on, right down the right few too.
Yeah, but that one's closed down.
Why they put no get bridge out there?
They could have to close that down itself. Uh-huh. But uh, punch, if they don't know, they know Kid Punch. I know, but if they shouldn't, his name is Ernest Miller.
Uh-huh.
But no one ever calls him Kid Punch.
Yes, I don't know anything come from. So Boyd told me that the last he saw Punch in the 11th East Band up north somewhere.
Oh yeah, he was working all those tent shows, you know, like Silas Green he was with for a long time. They'd go all around.
Punch, punch, punch, punch was it? Chomp it, chomp it, pan, down on Jesus have mercy, drink, liquor.
Oh, that's fine, huh?
You know the Buddy, let me see Buddy Pichy. That was, that was one. You know, good, huh?
I never knew Buddy, never met him.

Now, now, now one boy used to, you used to drink before, Lord, but when the food dumps in the morning, that the boy would die. And another one was playing across the river with me, George McCollum. That's the one who went to the, he took sick, he went to the doctor. And the doctor told him, don't take a drink and nothing at all with alcohol. So we got over there. That was my job. A fellow, a white-callowed clown, he would take a drink and take a drink and take a drink. And he was playing with a fellow by the name of Leon. He was playing with a fellow by the name of Leon, he was at Lafitte, crossed the river, every Saturday. He was a deputy sheriff, a fellow by the name of Leon. He was there, and the doctor told George Don Trinch, nothing with alcohol, you know. So we got over there. That was my job. A fellow, a white-callowed clown, he would take a drink. He had a cubit. The town, we did over there, the first thing with the units, the hole was on this side, and the volume was on this side. All that was his place. All right, Joe, go put the mastermind up and come and get your stuff. I'll go there and do two glass and a pot of whiskey. They were six of us. All right, I passed everybody. He's one of my glass. But I jumped George. So when they start to pour the whiskey, George called me. He said, George. He said, what you call that? I said, what's that, George? He said, you got all that whiskey that you passed. You got all that whiskey. You got all that whiskey that you took me? I said, George, what you told me? He said, what did I told you? He said, when? I said, did you tell me that doctor, Dr. Adam? Dr. Adam said, you don't drink. I'm sorry, Mom. I'll take you down and you'll all get through. He told me if you don't drink, you don't drink that bottle. So I gave him the bottle and the glass and everything. Let him drink. And the first thing when I come to find out, you don't cook it. Me and my wife went down there. I went down there. The bottle of the bottle. The bottle of the bottle. He said, he told me he talked about him. I don't drink. He was singing here. And I remember the time, the place, right there, he used to practice that with the WPA band. Remember that? I heard talk of it. George would, one of the leader, trumpet playing that band. He used to practice right there next to that church there. I just started that big building. All the time George would be there that band. He was just that good a trumpet player. But he killed himself. And when we went down there, me and my wife, we went to the West, we went to the funeral. And everything, and poor wife was kind. He said, I didn't tell us. Was he strong?
What sort of style did he play?

Oh, he was a strong trumpet player. And a very young man, too. Very young man, too. Well put on. Brown skin boy. Everybody was crazy. Smart boy. Can read music out this world. He killed himself. He killed himself. He killed himself. He watched the world. Every time I tell him about that little, he wanted to fight me. So I decided to let him go.
Did you play right time numbers and air music and stuff like that with him? Oh, yeah.

He used to play right time music. He crashed across the river. And then people used to treat us so. We used to make so much tape out there. Closer. That man was nice, too. Mr. Nunez. Leon Nunez. David Teixeira. Do they, uh... What about the dancers out there?
Were they different from the city? Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. They're different from the city.

Because you see them people don't care about the music like they do in the city. Especially them young. Them young, they are young. Them young, they are young. Them young, they are young. They sit down there. I can't say about the white, but the colored. The table. Oh, they're terrible in dance.
What kind of songs did the Cajuns like? I thought you know that. French people in Lafitte and times like that. What did they like?

Well, they used to like all the, you know, all good people used to play in the city. You know? A lot of them knew all that. Because a lot of them come in this city. Yeah. They know all that. All them kind of nice dance. They want nice waltz and blues and everything. Did they like French songs?
You play many French songs? Yes, that's right.

They got plenty Frenchmen back there too. They mixed up. They are playing so many fishmen and everything back there. Get crab and shrimp and fish and everything back there. They used to give us some to bring home. Did you tell them that I used to play with you, your old boy?
Mm-hmm.
Eh? Oh yes, brother. I believe you know that. You want to see this thing?
I believe you know it, guys. I see you. What's his name?
Guitar Fly.
Joe Silly. Do you see that? No, I don't know him. I know a trumpet player named Joe Pella. What do you say? Trumpet F된 stuff. I know there's a stuff like

I know the trumpet fly too. In New Jersey. My uncle will play electric guitar now. He used to play tenor banjos. Oh, I see. I'm not sure you'll see that old and old boy. I can tell you why you work there. Oh. You work at... Peter Armand.
Oh, I've heard of him. I know he used to drive them around.
He used to be the chauffeur there. The man blinding. The man what they said, he won so much money at them horses. One time.
Well, is he the same one that used to drive everybody around like he'd drive pehan around?

He must be. Must be because I remember one time, he come here, he told me that was his boss car. Automobile. I see. He told me he just had borrowed to come here. That was his boss car. Oh, I see. And they told me that man got some daughter working in that place. I don't forget on what street that place was. Oh, they were there. But I passed there one time. Peter Armand. I think it was Conti and Bergant. Right. Is that where you worked? Mm-hmm. Is that where you worked?
He worked that night or day or both? He worked that day.
But somebody told me... There's a young fella told me sometime ago, about a month ago, that he play three nights a week. Oh. Then, Mr. Wednesday, Wednesday Saturday and Sunday. I bet.
You have any other children that play music?
I got a boy playing drums, but I don't know why he has. Oh, is that right? He's been away from here. When he left here, he was playing drums.
And, uh, what about your father, your uncle, did any of you play music? No. You're the only one in your family, huh? You started it out. That's right. No.
Your grandson played, uh, play drums.
Oh, no, that must have... My daughter, uh, son, come right behind me, playing bass violin.
What is this guy?
Uh, uh, let me see. Miller, his last name. George Miller.
George Miller.
George Miller. Yeah. You want to know what they had?
He was out of California.
Uh-uh. That's the...
Uh-uh.
That's the place they called. Uh-uh. That's the place they called.
Uh-uh. Yeah, he went to Honolulu.
They were. They came back from Honolulu. That's the thing. Uh, you couldn't bass. They tell me you got a bass violin with the amplifier. Oh, I've seen that.
Yeah.

Yeah. Ricard is playing one of those, huh? Ricard. Ricard, no. Ricard Amplopom. No, that's another one. I know, long time when I first found out, I'm not playing many dance with him because he was playing trumpet. Uh-huh. And he got on the bass.
Yeah, how's he got to do?
Well, he got his jaw broke, I think, because what happened to him, I hurt. Uh-oh. Oh, Lord. I mean, that was years ago. Yeah, yeah.
I was surprised when they played me, Ricard. Ricard was playing, uh, for playing bass because Ricard was the first-class trumpet player. Mm-hmm.

Well, he still plays a little trumpet. He played Father Celestine's drum on trumpet. He's coming back, aren't you? Now he's mostly working. That's right. You don't like the way those young fellows play now? Uh-huh. You don't like the way the young fellows are playing now? Oh, them young ones coming now with them band?
Yeah. No, because they don't play nothing. What's the matter with them? Oh, but a whole lot of noise, and everybody wants to sing. They sing more than they play. You see?
The world is growing wise and weaker. Let me see.

Old time things are the way. There's very few Dixieland bands you can find in the city right now. That's right. Everything you find in them young people. And they got nice instruments and everything, but they don't play nothing but a whole lot of noise. Sing and how. But you see, when we get on the music stand, we have to play music. No, no, no, no, a whole lot of noise. Some people used to say long time ago, they used the high band to play music, not to sing. You have to put that music down.
What, did you ever have singers and entertainers with your bands in the old days? Oh, yeah.

Oh, yeah. Sometimes we had one or two. No, you got it. But not all I know it let them boys make it now. You see? We used to play three nights, three nights a week, gravel and rampant, at the Royal Garden. Right now I believe they got a market there. Right across the street from that story. Oh, yeah. I was playing there with Jack Kerris. Three nights a week. Wednesday, Saturday and Sunday. Jack Kerris.
Jack Kerris.

Trambone player. Used to live on 8 in front when he died. Three brothers. One named John. He was a trambone player. 된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된
and more. He died on California. That's right. That's right. That was another sweet trumpet player. All three of them died.
Do those young fellows study their music now or they just blow away?
Well, some of them don't do nothing but a whole lot of noise, you know. A whole lot of noise. They like that. Sing. But rather sound, you know. All kinds of sound. That's what the public like.
Did they use many mute to note bands like Jack Carrier's band when you worked with them?

They sometimes. Just sometimes. Sometimes. Jack used to care of mute all the time. And sometimes we had to tell him about it. Sometimes he used to get mad with me too. I said, what you care for? Well, he'd get to play sometime. I said, you could leave that mute home.

I know, that's one thing Mutt used to feature when he left here. That's right. He used to feature all different kind of mutes. And the same thing is true of Oliver. I just wondered if they used mutes, Danny.
Did Oliver use mutes much here? I think he did. He played so much. Oh Lord.
You said everybody, when Lewis played the blues, everybody really liked that.

Mm-hmm. You see Lewis, you're talking about Lewis Armstrong? Yeah. He used to play piano too. He did? He's a good piano player. Yeah, because he used to go to my watch. We used to get him to play on Saturday nights and have fish fry and put the lantern out and, you see, it'd be all along in downtown there on Saratoga, and Gravy. Well, the one in the biggest crowd would have music where they'd come. All of them? The people would fly there, you know. Oh yeah. So I had an old piano sitting in the dining room in them days and I used to get him over there and I'd breathe him well, you know. Where is that? In the battlefield you're talking about? No, that's on Saratoga between Gravy and Predee. That's long years ago. They tore on all that. I don't know where my house at, I think. Yeah. stuff

segments.chapter: Country years in St. John Parish
segments.title: Born in St. John Parish; the Magnolia Band and Casimir Matthews
segments.summary: Phillips was born in St. John Parish, left in 1918, and played guitar in the Magnolia Band led by his cousin Casimir Matthews.

segments.chapter: Country years in St. John Parish
segments.title: Towns played in the country parishes
segments.summary: He played St. James, St. John and St. Charles parishes and Allen mentions musicians from that area.

segments.chapter: Country years in St. John Parish
segments.title: Magnolia Band members and instruments
segments.summary: Seven-piece band with trumpet, trombone, clarinet, drums, guitar, and Phillips on bass violin.

segments.chapter: Country years in St. John Parish
segments.title: Playing by ear and starting young
segments.summary: Country bands mostly played by ear; Phillips started young, around 16, and Allen works out his birth year.

segments.chapter: Country years in St. John Parish
segments.title: Country music heard growing up: Laplace bands, blues
segments.summary: Laplace brass bands and dance bands played waltzes, card drills, ragtime and blues before he went to town.

segments.chapter: Country years in St. John Parish
segments.title: Pickwick band, Kid Thomas and the Hall family
segments.summary: He subbed with the Laplace Pickwick band, and talk turns to Kid Thomas and Edward Hall and his musician sons.

segments.chapter: Country years in St. John Parish
segments.title: Switching from guitar to bass, learned by himself
segments.summary: His cousin swapped him onto bass; he learned it by ear and toted it by buggy.

segments.chapter: Country years in St. John Parish
segments.title: Dances, society balls and picnics in the country
segments.summary: The band played society dances and big summer picnics under pecan trees for white and colored audiences.

segments.chapter: Country years in St. John Parish
segments.title: New Orleans bands hired for society banquets
segments.summary: Country societies hired New Orleans bands such as Kid Howard and Jack Carey only for the annual banquet.

segments.chapter: Country years in St. John Parish
segments.title: Country bass players and using the bow
segments.summary: Joe Robinet of Laplace was a bass reader; Phillips used a bow and only began plucking in New Orleans.

segments.chapter: Country years in St. John Parish
segments.title: Dajon trumpeters and the skiff drowning on the river
segments.summary: Trumpeter Dajon helped him, and a Laplace band's skiff capsized in a storm crossing the river on the way to a dance.

segments.chapter: Country years in St. John Parish
segments.title: Kid Ory and geography of St. John, St. James
segments.summary: Talk of Kid Ory in the country, the parish seat, and small bands in St. John and St. James parishes.

segments.chapter: Country years in St. John Parish
segments.title: Why he moved to the city
segments.summary: He left because of family trouble and because his family was already in town.

segments.chapter: Coming to the city, Celestin and Armstrong
segments.title: George Foster, riverboats, and last dance with Celestin and Armstrong
segments.summary: Phillips played dances with Celestin and played the last dance with Louis Armstrong in the Tuxedo band before Armstrong left.

segments.chapter: Coming to the city, Celestin and Armstrong
segments.title: Tuxedo band personnel and Bebe Ridgley; Armstrong's last night
segments.summary: Bebe Ridgley played trombone; Phillips recounts bass player Jimmy Johnson falling ill and his last job with Armstrong.

segments.chapter: Coming to the city, Celestin and Armstrong
segments.title: Armstrong as second trumpet to Celestin
segments.summary: Armstrong played second trumpet, soft and between Celestin's phrases, content to be a sideman for money; Phillips' wife knew him.

segments.chapter: Natchez fire
segments.title: Walter Barnes band fire in Mississippi
segments.summary: Allen raises the Mississippi band that burned in a dance hall fire, leading to the wife's account.

segments.chapter: Natchez fire
segments.title: Natchez baby doll dance fire details
segments.summary: Mrs. Phillips and Phillips describe the nailed windows, one door, scalding tin roof, a priest, and the bass player who walked out.

segments.chapter: City bands, Mississippi and baseball trips
segments.title: Playing with Charlie Love and Kid Thomas across the river
segments.summary: Reel 2 begins; Phillips played with trumpeter Love and Thomas at a night club across the river, and Allen mentions Toots Johnson in Baton Rouge.

segments.chapter: City bands, Mississippi and baseball trips
segments.title: Kid Rene and Kid Howard
segments.summary: Phillips played a long time with Kid Rene's band, and Allen shares impressions of Rene and Howard.

segments.chapter: City bands, Mississippi and baseball trips
segments.title: Sam Morgan's band and the Morgan brothers
segments.summary: He played with Sam Morgan's popular band; the brothers Isaiah, Andrew, Albert and Sam are discussed.

segments.chapter: City bands, Mississippi and baseball trips
segments.title: Playing in Mississippi towns
segments.summary: He played in Harrisburg, Biloxi and other Mississippi towns, with a Dude and Foster trio mentioned.

segments.chapter: City bands, Mississippi and baseball trips
segments.title: Trip with the Pelican baseball team and playing at ball games
segments.summary: Band went with the Pelicans to play two games and played at ballparks, including between innings.

segments.chapter: King Oliver era and Punch
segments.title: Baseball park dances and Chicken Powell's Saturday dances
segments.summary: Mrs. Phillips recalls dances after ball games and Chicken Powell's Saturday dances for the colored workers.

segments.chapter: King Oliver era and Punch
segments.title: Henry Zeno and King Oliver with the big eye
segments.summary: Mrs. Phillips' cousin Zeno drummed in the Eagle Band; they discuss Oliver, his eye, and musicians who followed him.

segments.chapter: King Oliver era and Punch
segments.title: Frankie Duson and dances with quadrilles
segments.summary: Frankie Duson's trombone playing and the quadrille and shotis dances; also Joe Oliver and Buddy Petit.

segments.chapter: King Oliver era and Punch
segments.title: Racial mixing in the music, Punch Miller and Page Hotel
segments.summary: Allen and Mrs. Phillips talk about mixed-race groups and segregation; Punch Miller's whereabouts and name.

segments.chapter: Cajun dances and family
segments.title: George McCollum, the trumpeter who killed himself, and Lafitte gig
segments.summary: Story of George McCollum, a trumpeter playing with Phillips at Lafitte, his drinking and suicide.

segments.chapter: Cajun dances and family
segments.title: Cajun audiences across the river; trumpeter Peter Armand
segments.summary: Dancers across the river, their taste in waltzes and blues, and a chauffeur-trumpeter named Armand.

segments.chapter: Cajun dances and family
segments.title: Phillips' family musicians and Ricard changing to bass
segments.summary: His son plays bass, grandson drums; talk of bass amplifiers and Ricard Alexis switching from trumpet.

segments.chapter: Reflections and Armstrong
segments.title: Young players today, the Royal Garden and Armstrong at the piano
segments.summary: Phillips dislikes modern bands that sing, recalls Royal Garden with Jack Carey and mutes, and Mrs. Phillips remembers Armstrong playing piano.
